column5: F: Before we start: what did the owner build back in twenty twelve? | M: This is the owner's own diagram: the ERP, an ActiveMQ message queue in the middle, and the POS. Three stacks that work asynchronously. The queue only holds the data, and it is a server you install and run.

column5: F: And what is different now? | M: The same three stacks, still delayed: the end of day goes up and the start of day comes down. The till is a browser tab that keeps working offline, the middle is a plain mailbox with no server to run, and head office is a browser, or the original iDempiere.

column5: F: So what does a whole shop look like? | M: The till stack opens up into a branch. Several tills, each air-gapped on its own localhost, with no public address. | F: And how do they work together? | M: A small branch relay inside the shop joins them. It carries only the shop's own traffic. | F: Then who does talk to head office? | M: Only the main till. It holds head office's stock figure and collects the others' order lines. Its end of day goes up and the start of day comes down. If the branch relay is down, every till keeps selling.

column5: F: Several tills, several closings. What does head office hear from them? | M: Nothing while they sell. Each till rings on its own, on its own localhost. The main till collects the others' order lines inside the branch, by timestamp, and never a line twice.
column6: F: Several tills, several closings. What does head office hear from them? | M: Nothing while they sell. Each till rings on its own, on its own localhost. The main till collects the others' order lines inside the branch, by timestamp, and never a line twice.

column5: F: So who does talk to head office? | M: Only the main till, and only once. Its end of day is the single send to the internet relay, and head office picks it up from there. Its running record starts from head office's stock figure and takes off every collected line.

column5: F: And at head office, the next morning? | M: A single click on Branch Day Close. It imports the day's sales and runs the replenishment, in the same order the clerk would.

column5: F: How many steps did that used to take? | M: Twenty-eight clicks across six screens. Now nine clicks on one screen. That count is read off the menu path, not from a recording. | F: Same books? | M: Row for row. In the checked test the difference from doing it step by step is zero, and a bill-of-materials item sold at the till takes its parts out of stock: six, twenty-four and fifteen hundred.

column5: F: How does a price change reach the tills? | M: In the morning batch, and only what changed. One price edited at head office sends one row. The twenty-six others stay as they were.

column5: F: And receiving stock? | M: Five were sent, three arrived, one was scrapped. The confirmation rides along with the next end-of-day send. Head office stock goes from twenty to fifteen, and the store from four to six.

column5: F: What is not built yet? | M: Four things. Legacy writes nine point zero in a text where we write nine, a difference we have not accepted and will fix on our side. The price-change timestamp could not be compared, because legacy's web service cannot edit that table. A pair of tills sharing a table over a real relay is not proven yet. And memory with all the pictures loaded is not measured.
